pronunciation.ipaLabel: Conventional reading — Arabic name of the temple town

phonemes.desc: From Arabic al-qirq? — the accepted reading is “the fortified village” (Egyptian pr-ḳrnrq, “the sanctuary of the horizon’s entrance”).
The name of the place became the name of the god’s dwelling — a temple-city theophany.

kin.label: Egyptian
kin.form: Ipet-isut “the Most Select of Places” — Karnak’s ancient name

pronunciation.note: Unlike most names in the lexicon, this one entered via Arabic — the temple’s town-name, fossilised.

domains.title: The Fortified Village, Temple of Amun
domains.subtitle: Ipet-isut, the Most Select of Places
domains.lead: Karnak is not a god but a god’s address: the ‘fortified village’ whose ancient Egyptian name — Ipet-isut, ‘the Most Select of Places’ — declared it the estate where Amun-Ra kept his chosen ground. As a lexicon entry it stands for the temple-complex itself, the largest religious structure ever built, accumulated by thirty pharaohs over two thousand years.

cards.name: The Great Hypostyle
cards.desc: A forest of 134 columns under one roof — the largest columned hall ever raised.

cards.name: House of Amun-Ra
cards.desc: The god’s ‘mansion’ on earth; the cult image dwelt here in a daily liturgy of waking, washing, and feeding.

cards.name: The Pharaohs’ Ledger
cards.desc: Every dynasty added a pylon, an obelisk, a hall — the temple is Egypt’s history carved in sequence.

cards.name: The Sacred Lake
cards.desc: Its rectangular lake staged the primeval waters for the priests’ dawn ablutions.

mythology.lead: Karnak’s ‘mythology’ is architectural: every pylon is a cosmogonic statement, every obelisk a frozen sunbeam, every festival route a replay of the gods’ first processions. The complex’s ancient name, Ipet-isut, names the selection of this ground out of all possible grounds — the one place the god chose.

myths.title: The Most Select of Places
myths.text: The temple theology held that Amun’s staff, planted in the ground of Thebes at the world’s beginning, designated Ipet-isut as his estate — ‘the most select of places’. Each new king’s building programme was framed not as innovation but as the staff’s ancient will, finally fulfilled.

myths.title: The River Journey of the Gods
myths.text: In the great Opet festival, Amun’s barque sailed the canal from Karnak to Luxor temple and back — the Theban gods’ annual renewal of their own marriage with the city. The avenue of ram-headed sphinxes, restored today, was the procession’s road; the festival’s reliefs cover Karnak’s walls.

myths.title: The Pharaohs’ Roll Call
myths.text: Seti I’s gallery of kings, the Karnak King List, names the legitimate succession from the ancestors — a theology of history in stone, in which every true king is one who kept the ‘Most Select of Places’ in repair. The list omits the heretics, editing eternity.

myths.title: From Sand to Science
myths.text: Cleared by the French expedition of 1799, Karnak became the first Egyptian temple to be systematically published — the Description de l’Égypte’s plates fixed its image in the world’s imagination. Champollion walked its halls reading the walls aloud; the decipherment of Egypt effectively happened here.

lore.syncretism: Karnak housed them all: Amun-Ra supreme, but also Montu, Mut, Khonsu, Ptah and Opet, in a polyphony of chapels that makes the complex a pantheon in plan. The Greeks called the whole Thebes ‘Diospolis’, city of Zeus-Amun; the temple was the Zeus-estate, and Alexander the Great crossed the desert to its oracle to be confirmed son of Amun.
lore.culturalLegacy: The hypostyle hall’s columns seeded every ‘Egyptian’ column in the world’s architecture — railway stations, museums, mausoleums. The Sound-and-Light economy of modern Luxor, and half of every coffee-table book on Egypt, rest on this one complex; its restoration is an ongoing international project two centuries old.
lore.extendedMeditation: A place-name standing among god-names: Karnak’s inclusion in the lexicon is deliberate — the temple-city as deity, the dwelling as theophany. Its plain ASCII spelling is the one every language already uses; the fortified village needed no restoration because the whole world never stopped saying its name.

Opet festival reliefs, Luxor and Karnak
Barguet, Le temple d’Amon-Rê à Karnak

lore.archaeology: Two thousand years of continuous building: the Middle Kingdom precursors, Hatshepsut’s obelisks, the great hypostyle of Seti I and Ramesses II, the sacred lake, the seven processional pylons, the Khonsu temple — all standing and all published. The ‘Avenue of Sphinxes’ to Luxor has been re-excavated in the twenty-first century.
lore.cult: The daily cult of Amun-Ra — the god’s waking, washing, robing and feeding — was the most elaborate liturgy of Egypt, performed by the highest-ranking priests of the realm. The great festivals of Opet and the Valley moved the god’s barques between temples with the whole city watching.
lore.iconography: Karnak has no divine image — its icon is the ground-plan: pylons ranked like sunset gates, obelisks like ray-shafts, the columned hall as a petrified papyrus thicket. The ram-headed criosphinx, Amun’s processional animal, lines the temple’s approaches.
lore.reception: For two centuries Karnak has been the default image of ‘ancient temple’ in world culture — from Belzoni’s moving of its statues to the British Museum, to its role in every film that needs Egypt. Its name entered every major language unchanged, a loan-word from the largest religious building humanity ever raised.
